motion: Do human beings have free will?

bridges.description: Establish that deterministic causation is compatible with the kind of free will worth having.
Connect responsiveness to reasons, foresight, and self-control to agency and responsibility.
Explain free will as an evolved skill strengthened by education and social institutions.
Show how graded capacities support fair, humane, and instrumental accountability practices.
Argue that choices do not constitute free will because agents did not control the causes that formed their chooser and values.
Trace behavior through an unbroken biological and environmental history rather than an independent source of action.
Treat self-control itself as a biologically developed trait whose distribution is not chosen.
Connect reduced responsibility judgments to less cruel institutions while retaining instrumental protection and incentives.

sections.title: Causal origins of agency
sections.rationale: The central clash begins with whether present intention and reasons-responsiveness suffice, or whether freedom requires control over the history that formed the intending agent.

sections.title: Evolved self-control and reasons
sections.rationale: Dennett identifies free will with an evolved capacity for foresight, reliability, reasons, and self-control; Sapolsky argues that this capacity is itself biologically caused.

sections.title: Responsibility and humane institutions
sections.rationale: Both accept instrumental sanctions but dispute whether responsibility remains justified and whether moral progress reflects improved accountability or subtraction of blame.

sections.title: Quotation, interpretation, and intuition
sections.rationale: The live exchange over the machine passage, runner analogy, two-stage model, and intuition bears directly on how each side represents and supports the rival conception.

sections.title: Determinism, choice, and unpredictability
sections.rationale: The parties agree that options and choices occur but dispute whether deterministic chaos and uncontrollable variation leave room for autonomy once the chooser's values are causally formed.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Ordinary intention, alternatives, and absence of coercion do not by themselves establish free will.
moves.warrant: Present choice is only the end of the causal story; the prior question is how the person became someone who would form that intention.
moves.inference: Responsibility cannot be grounded merely in the phenomenology or legal surface features of choosing.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Sapolsky's explicit thesis and includes the complete intent-and-movie analogy through his statement of the upstream question.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator explicitly hands the opening to Robert, and uninterrupted first-person continuity identifies Sapolsky throughout.
moves.importanceRationale: This states the con side's central criterion and the question every later causal example is meant to answer.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly denies that an occurrent choice supplies the originating control required for free will.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Choices emerge from interacting conditions ranging from current physiology through development and fetal life.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky cites immediate states, hormones, trauma, childhood adversity and culture, and fetal stress or nutrition as mechanisms affecting judgment and executive control.
moves.inference: The agent's present decision-making capacities are products of an inherited causal history rather than self-created starting points.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This long but unified span follows Sapolsky's declared biological hierarchy from immediate states through childhood, culture, and fetal development; ending earlier would omit a major level of the same cumulative warrant.
moves.attributionRationale: This is continuous speech within Sapolsky's formally introduced opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It supplies the principal empirical-style causal chain supporting the con account of agency.

burdenContact.rationale: The examples connect present executive control to unchosen conditions across several timescales.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Genes, culture, and prior biology operate as interacting parts of one continuous causal history.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky rejects genetic isolation, describes genes as shaping responses to environments, extends the history through ancestral culture, and says these levels form a continuous biological arc.
moves.inference: No temporal level in the described history supplies an independent break where free will enters.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Sapolsky's express rejection of genetic fundamentalism and preserves the complete genes-environment, ancestral-culture, luck-amplification, and continuous-arc synthesis.
moves.attributionRationale: Sapolsky supplies the substantive argument throughout; a brief moderator one-more-minute reminder is mixed into the span but contributes no argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It integrates the separate causal levels into the con side's continuous-history account and explicitly avoids simple genetic determinism.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that interacting biological and environmental causes leave no independent causal gap.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Free-will advocates must show action independent of biological and environmental history.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky says known causal influences form a continuous arc with no demonstrated break and challenges the opposing side to identify an independent action.
moves.inference: Absent such evidence, the default should be doubt rather than belief in free will.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Sapolsky's explicit challenge after completing the causal hierarchy and retains the complete burden allocation and stated default.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Sapolsky opening ending immediately before the moderator's poll report.
moves.importanceRationale: This converts the causal survey into the con side's express motion-level burden and conclusion.

burdenContact.rationale: It states what evidence Sapolsky believes is necessary to establish free will and why he thinks it is absent.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Determinism and free will can coexist when free will is understood as receptivity to reasons rather than independence from all prior influence.
moves.warrant: Dennett notes that argument can convince people, accepts unequal hormonal and developmental starting material, and describes free will as a social system that reduces those disadvantages while cultivating reliability and self-control.
moves.inference: Causal history does not disqualify agency if people can respond to reasons and develop dependable control.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts at Dennett's formal opening answer and ends after his compact definition of reliability and self-control, preserving his concession about unequal causal starting points.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: I believe in both determinism and free will.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator names Dan at the handoff, followed by continuous first-person argument in Dennett's opening.
moves.importanceRationale: This directly answers the con criterion and states the pro side's central compatibilist alternative.

burdenContact.rationale: It supplies the pro definition under which determination by prior causes does not negate freedom.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Free will is an evolved suite of skills for self-control, foresight, and reliable conduct.
moves.warrant: Dennett traces increasing competence from early life through civilization and contrasts humans' ability to foresee and prevent harm with a tree's lack of such capacities.
moves.inference: Degrees of developed control can ground meaningful freedom without any metaphysical exemption from causation.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the complete evolutionary-skill argument from the origin of competence through civilization's distillation of self-control and the foresight contrast.
moves.attributionRationale: Uninterrupted Dennett opening with consistent first-person and subject continuity.
moves.importanceRationale: It provides the positive pro account of what free will is and how it arises.

burdenContact.rationale: The evolutionary and civilizational account links ordinary capacities to the claimed freedom.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Responsibility depends on sufficient self-control and can be withheld when capacity is diminished.
moves.warrant: Dennett distinguishes adequately self-controlled adults from people who should not drive or cannot manage contracts and acknowledges an inevitably somewhat arbitrary threshold.
moves.inference: A capacity-based account can recognize luck, impairment, and loss of free will without abandoning responsibility for everyone.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This span begins with the wiring and driving examples and includes the full threshold, diminished-capacity, and loss-of-control qualification through the achievement definition.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: Free will is an achievement. It's a skill.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Dennett speech with no ambiguous ownership apart from routine caption overlap.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the main pro answer to inequality and impairment while preserving a responsibility category.

burdenContact.rationale: It grounds accountability in assessed capacity and explicitly exempts people below the threshold.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Civilization has improved responsibility practices by discarding horrific punishment and theological guilt.
moves.warrant: Dennett points to historical movement away from drawing and quartering and from barbaric notions of guilt.
moves.inference: Keeping a naturalized free-will framework need not preserve cruel or medieval blame.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The selected events capture Dennett's complete moral-progress point from his praise of Sapolsky's history through the explicit rejection of horrific punishment and guilt.
moves.attributionRationale: The passage remains within Dennett's uninterrupted opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It addresses the practical humanitarian burden shared by both speakers, though it is not the primary definition of free will.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that accountability institutions can evolve away from cruelty while remaining functional.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Free will has grown with evolved self-control, and an undetermined will would not be worth wanting.
moves.warrant: Dennett describes increasing capacities to control ourselves and each other and says wills should be determined by facts and values.
moves.inference: Deterministic formation by relevant reasons can constitute, rather than defeat, worthwhile freedom.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins at Dennett's explicit evolutionary summation and runs through his complete contrast between an undetermined will and determination by facts and values.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: We want our will to be determined by the facts and by our values.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Dennett opening, with no handoff until after the subsequent machine passage.
moves.importanceRationale: This gives the pro side's direct answer to why determinism does not remove the freedom at issue.

burdenContact.rationale: It directly presents determination by facts and values as compatible with valuable agency.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Being an evolved machine does not prevent good or bad things from happening to a person.
moves.warrant: Dennett identifies himself as a machine made of machines while maintaining that he can still fare well or badly.
moves.inference: A mechanistic account of humans alone does not eliminate welfare or the meaningful capacities associated with free will.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This retains Dennett's introduction of Sapolsky's machine statement, his entire machine-and-welfare response, and his concluding interpretation.
moves.attributionRationale: Dennett explicitly introduces the quotation and then speaks in the first person through the end of his opening.
moves.importanceRationale: It tests whether mechanistic description has the normative implications Dennett attributes to Sapolsky's wording.

burdenContact.rationale: The move resists an inference from machine status to the absence of normatively significant human capacities.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Sapolsky's machine statement did not deny that less pain and more happiness are good.
moves.warrant: He supplies the omitted continuation saying that, at his core, lives with less pain and more happiness are good; Dennett acknowledges the addendum.
moves.inference: The mechanistic con position should not be treated as eliminating human welfare.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts with Sapolsky's substantive response, includes the challenged quotation and its complete qualification, and includes Dennett's brief acknowledgment as contextual confirmation rather than as Sapolsky's words.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator hands the reply to Robert, and auxiliary audio text confirms Sapolsky's qualification; zero-based event 615 is Dennett's brief contextual acknowledgment, not Sapolsky speech.
moves.importanceRationale: This correction prevents a material misstatement of the con position's practical implications.

burdenContact.rationale: The restored qualification preserves welfare improvement as a con-side normative aim.

responseComponents.description: Restores the immediate qualification omitted from the machine quotation and accepts that welfare can improve.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Rejecting free will is compatible with using punishment and reward instrumentally.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky expressly says both speakers agree that these tools are permissible for their effects.
moves.inference: The con view does not entail abandoning public protection, incentives, or behavioral intervention.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: These events contain the complete explicit common-ground statement and end as Sapolsky turns to the disputed evolutionary issue.
moves.attributionRationale: Sapolsky continues his reply; the auxiliary audio text separately confirms the same speaker and words.
moves.importanceRationale: It answers a central practical concern about the consequences of rejecting responsibility.

burdenContact.rationale: It preserves protective and incentive functions while separating them from desert-based blame.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the instrumental reform aim while preparing to dispute that it shows an increase in free will.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Historical moral progress has often come from recognizing less responsibility, not more free will.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky cites witches, epilepsy, and dyslexia as cases where causal understanding displaced blame and cruel treatment.
moves.inference: The humane trajectory invoked by Dennett supports continued subtraction of responsibility from causal misfortune.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts at Sapolsky's explicit answer to Dennett's evolutionary-progress point and includes all three examples through the humane conclusion.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Sapolsky reply with clear address to Dan and stable first-person framing.
moves.importanceRationale: This reverses Dennett's practical-progress argument and links the con theory to institutional reform.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that causal explanation has improved institutions by reducing blame.

responseComponents.description: Reinterprets the same decline in cruel punishment as evidence of reduced attributions of responsibility.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Self-control is a biological trait, not a freely supplied use of otherwise unchosen attributes.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky identifies prefrontal development as a basis of control and cites early socioeconomic conditions as predictors of that development.
moves.inference: Differences in gumption and executive control cannot independently ground desert because the capacities themselves arise from luck and environment.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This extended span preserves the full false-dichotomy setup, biological account of self-control, childhood socioeconomic example, and resulting conclusion about later decisions.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: self-control is as biological of a trait as is your eye color.
moves.attributionRationale: This is continuous Sapolsky reply; the odd word 'courtesies' is caption recognition noise, so it is not used as a featured quotation.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly attacks the capacity that carries most of Dennett's constructive case.

burdenContact.rationale: It treats reasons-responsive control as another caused and unequally distributed biological ability.

responseComponents.description: Accepts that self-control exists but argues its biological origin prevents it from supplying ultimate control.
Challenges the distinction between assigned traits and the allegedly responsible use of those traits.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Dennett's reported runner analogy appears to attach desert to overcoming an initial disadvantage.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky quotes the analogy and reads failure to overcome bad luck as a moral judgment that insufficient gumption does not deserve success.
moves.inference: A free-will account based on control risks treating biologically caused capacities as morally self-created.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span includes the full live quotation of the runner analogy, Sapolsky's interpretation, and his explicit disagreement without extending into the separate intuition argument.
moves.attributionRationale: Sapolsky explicitly labels the passage as a quotation from Dan and then clearly marks his own interpretation.
moves.importanceRationale: It is a concrete textual challenge to the role of luck and desert in Dennett's position.

burdenContact.rationale: The move argues that overcoming disadvantage depends on caused capacities rather than independent control.

responseComponents.description: Challenges the desert implications of treating evolved control skills as achievements attributable to the agent.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Intuition is an unreliable guide to free will and responsibility.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky says past intuitions supported slavery, child labor, and blame for dyslexia, and that growing causal knowledge repeatedly displaced those judgments.
moves.inference: A model's fit with authorship intuitions supplies little support when those intuitions may encode mistaken responsibility judgments.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span retains the two-stage-model quotation, the express attack on intuition, multiple historical and medical examples, and the concluding institutional implication.
quoteEligibleExactSpans: intuition is a really lousy guide for thinking about how the world works.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Sapolsky reply with explicit quotation markers separating Dennett's reported words from Sapolsky's argument.
moves.importanceRationale: It challenges an identified support for a free-will model and broadens the con case about moral learning.

burdenContact.rationale: It links correction of responsibility intuitions to less punitive and more accurate social treatment.

responseComponents.description: Challenges reliance on intuitive authorship as support for models intended to explain worthwhile freedom.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: The runner and two-stage passages, as Dennett reports their contexts, do not endorse the views Sapolsky attributes to him.
moves.warrant: Dennett says the runner passage immediately calls the analogy misleading and the article rejects the two-stage model despite noting that it meets an intuition.
moves.inference: Sapolsky's textual challenges do not establish that Dennett grounds responsibility in overcoming luck or endorses that decision model.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span starts at Dennett's formal reply, includes both complete context corrections, and ends after his explicit distinction between meeting an intuition and supporting the model.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator names Dan, and auxiliary audio text confirms the wording and speaker of both context corrections.
moves.importanceRationale: It is the direct reply to two source-based attacks that otherwise materially characterize the pro theory.

burdenContact.rationale: The correction protects the pro account from being assessed as the runner-desert or two-stage theory it disclaims.

responseComponents.description: Says the cited text continues by rejecting the runner framing as misleading.
Distinguishes acknowledging that a model meets an intuition from endorsing that model.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Compatibilist freedom needs complex unpredictability and resistance to manipulation, not indeterminism.
moves.warrant: Dennett invokes chaotic, hard-to-predict brain activity and says mature responsible people can resist being turned into puppets, while conceding they did not choose to become such people and cannot always resist.
moves.inference: A causally formed person can still possess operational autonomy in the face of present influence.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with the quoted educational claim, preserves Dennett's compatibilist correction, and includes his complete autonomy claim with its express origin and reliability qualifications.
moves.attributionRationale: Continuous Dennett reply; first-person and direct address remain clear despite automatic-caption fillers.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the most developed reply defining what deterministic autonomy adds beyond mere causation.

burdenContact.rationale: It explains the freedom-making capacity available within a deterministic system.

responseComponents.description: Rejects causal independence as the criterion and substitutes resistance to present control.
Recasts the dispute as a definitional and functional compatibilist claim rather than reliance on indeterminism.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Sapolsky already values and exercises the kind of self-regulation Dennett calls free will.
moves.warrant: Dennett points to Sapolsky's effort to understand and manage his own mental difficulties and to his educational project about behavioral causes.
moves.inference: Their disagreement may concern the label and an incompatibilist definition more than the desirability of the underlying capacity.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: This concise span contains Dennett's complete argument from Sapolsky's acknowledged striving and achievement to the definitional disagreement about indeterminism.
moves.attributionRationale: Dennett continues uninterrupted and explicitly addresses Robert and his book.
moves.importanceRationale: It attempts to establish common ground around the central capacity even if the term remains disputed.

burdenContact.rationale: It identifies reflective self-regulation as a real and desired human competence.

responseComponents.description: Concedes causal formation but argues that Sapolsky still values and exercises the resulting control capacity.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Evolution and agency can use uncontrollable variation without requiring metaphysical indeterminism.
moves.warrant: Dennett distinguishes determined but uncontrollable coin flips from control by an agent and says natural selection works with deterministic chaos.
moves.inference: Appealing to evolved option generation does not show that determinism rules out free will.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins at Dennett's explicit incompatibilism charge and preserves the full coin-flip, uncontrollability, variation, and deterministic-chaos distinction.
moves.attributionRationale: Dennett retains the floor through the moderator's subsequent invitation to Robert.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly separates determinism from predictability and frames the final exchange over option generation.

burdenContact.rationale: It blocks the inference from deterministic evolution to the absence of usable variation or freedom.

responseComponents.description: Argues that deterministic causal history can still generate uncontrollable diversity and thus does not decide the motion by itself.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.claim: Generating and choosing among options does not yield free will when the chooser's values were not chosen.
moves.warrant: Sapolsky accepts chaotic option production, filtering, weighing, reflection, and genuine choice, but asks how the person became one who would rank and select those options.
moves.inference: More sophisticated decision machinery relocates rather than answers the question of originating control.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins at Sapolsky's invited direct answer and retains his complete concession about option generation and choice through the return to unchosen values and character.
moves.attributionRationale: The moderator explicitly invites Robert; the answer remains his until Dennett addresses him by name.
moves.importanceRationale: This is the con side's direct final answer to Dennett's deterministic-chaos challenge.

burdenContact.rationale: It accepts ordinary choosing while denying that the agent controlled the formation of the chooser.

responseComponents.description: Accepts generated variation but argues that selection among options still expresses unchosen values and character.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Education and treatment can counteract causal disadvantages, while persistent incapacity can excuse rather than erase freedom universally.
moves.warrant: Dennett agrees that history formed people but argues civilization learns to remedy some effects and withhold responsibility from children, senile people, and people with brain damage.
moves.inference: Causal origin and luck are compatible with later acquisition of responsibility-capable agency by many people.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span begins with Dennett's acknowledgment of the shared long history and includes the complete counteraction, treatment, exception, education, and responsibility argument.
moves.attributionRationale: Dennett resumes by addressing Robert and continues without a handoff.
moves.importanceRationale: It directly answers the con claim that causal formation removes agency from every chooser.

burdenContact.rationale: It argues that social intervention can build or restore the capacities constituting free will.

responseComponents.description: Accepts the causal history but says education and treatment can counteract some of its effects.
Treats biological impairment as grounds for graded excuse rather than universal abolition of responsibility.
Maintains that a causally formed chooser can later acquire the competence to take responsibility.

moves.speaker: Daniel Dennett
moves.claim: Civilization needs law and punishment, but the ideal sanction system is fair and non-awful.
moves.warrant: Dennett invokes the necessity of law and order and explicitly qualifies the ideal system by fairness and minimized suffering.
moves.inference: Responsibility can serve instrumental social coordination without endorsing gratuitous cruelty.
moves.sourceSpanSelectionRationale: The span contains the final formal-round punishment argument through the clear fair-and-non-awful qualification; the recognition-corrupted final clause is retained as boundary evidence but not quoted or interpreted.
moves.attributionRationale: Dennett's ownership is clear, but the last captioned clause is recognition-corrupted; the selected claim relies only on the clear preceding wording.
moves.audioVerificationReason: Verify the recognition-corrupted final clause from the prescribed source-audio boundary clip before downstream editorial use.
moves.importanceRationale: It closes the formal exchange on the shared institutional question while preserving Dennett's humanitarian limitation.

burdenContact.rationale: It states the practical form that justified accountability should take.

responseComponents.description: Builds on the shared acceptance of instrumental sanctions.
Answers the humane-treatment concern by limiting sanctions to a fair and non-awful system.

selectedMajorLines.description: Sapolsky's opening distinction between choosing and control over the origins of intention.
Sapolsky's multiscale biological and environmental causal hierarchy and burden challenge.
Dennett's compatibilist definition through reasons, evolved self-control, and graded capacity.
The competing interpretations of humane historical change and instrumental sanction.
The machine quotation, runner analogy, two-stage model, and intuition disputes with live corrections.
The dispute over whether biological self-control and unchosen capacities ground responsibility.
The deterministic-chaos and option-generation exchange, including Sapolsky's acceptance of actual choice.

coverageAudit.moderatorTreatment: The moderator supplies logistics and handoffs only in the retained formal window; no moderator statement is selected as a third-side argument.
coverageAudit.qualificationPreservation: The inventory preserves Sapolsky's acceptance of ordinary intention, choice, biological self-control, welfare, and instrumental sanctions, and Dennett's acceptance of determinism, luck, diminished capacity, exceptions, and humane punishment.

handoffs.basis: Named reply invitation and direct address to Dan.

selectionBalanceAudit.rationale: The one-move total difference and all one-move section differences arise from distinct source arguments and remain below the frozen thresholds.

sections.rationale: Three con moves distinguish the origin criterion, multiscale causal evidence, and express burden challenge; the two pro moves give the initial compatibilist answer and final institutional response.
The section retains the positive evolved-skill account, the biological-control challenge, and the pro common-ground reply.
The selected rows separately cover capacity thresholds, historical reform, instrumental agreement, the con reversal, and the final fair-sanction position.
Rows preserve each live quotation challenge and correction without exceeding publication capacity.
Rows distinguish worthwhile determination, causal continuity through genes and culture, chaotic autonomy, evolution's variation, and the final option-selection answer.
